title: The Juneteenth haircut lie and being called Hamburger Red
summary: Cobb tells how he spent his haircut money, lied to his mother, was kept from the Emancipation Park festival, and learned never to lie; his hamburger habit earned him the nickname Hamburger Red.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Where I came from: parents, siblings and birth

blocks.x: PROCEEDINGS
Okay now, we're just going back to -- earlier we talking about emancipation day, June the 19th?
Yeah, 19th of June -- June-teenth, we call it here.
June-teenth.
June-teenth.
And now, you have another memory of that when you were a youngster, okay?
Right.
Why don't you tell --

As I was saying to you, Stanley, that my mother gave me money for a haircut, a dollar, and I didn't get the haircut from where I supposed to get it to go to the June-teenth Festival with my cousins and what have you. And I went to a friend, and he was going to cut my hair for me. We were going to take the money and split it, 50-50, 50 cents a piece.

And he started to cutting on my hair and got one side up, and his mother came in, and he hadn't washed the dishes. So he had to leave me in the bathroom. So -- my mother's here. He went to wash the dishes and try to take care of his chores, and I had to slip out the front door when he let me know when to go. And when my mother came home that night, she asked me, did I get a haircut. I say, sure, lying.

She said, who cut it? I said, Mr. Harris. That was my barber. Uh-huh. Are you sure Mr. Harris cut it? Yes, he did. She didn't say anything to me now other than I couldn't go to the Emancipation Park the next day because I lied to her. And she told me one thing. She said, I can't stand a liar because anybody that'll lie will steal, and I can't stand a liar and I can't stand a thief.

And she punished me. She didn't whip me for it. She punished me by not letting me go, and everybody left me the next day, but I told the lady next door that we were ready -- my mother was ready for her, and she called my mother on the job where she was working, and she said, I'm sorry he told you, but he didn't tell me. And she wouldn't let me go. But she begged and pleaded for me, but it didn't work.

But as I said to you before, she was as hurt for doing it, but she had to stand on her own convictions, and she knew I liked hamburgers because everybody called me Hamburger Red. That's another one of my nicknames.
Hamburger Red?
That's right.
Because --
Because I love hamburger. I really did.
Oh, I see.
And we had a place, man, that hamburger was the best in town, and I was on my way to the theater, I

would stop and get one. Neither here nor there, what I'm saying, she sent me down to get a dozen hamburgers. And I had a free ride. My man would take me free. Four cents was all it was. Then let me drive the streetcar on a long strip. Then knowing he was coming back on the route, I waited for him. So that means with the eight cents I had round trip, I had a nickel to get me another hamburger and three pennies left over.
(Laughter)

My mother gave me 68 cents. 60 -- for the hamburgers, nickel a piece, a dozen. And the other eight cents was for the round trip. And she wanted to make me happy even after I spent the day rolling an automobile tire up and down the sidewalk. That was my recreation for that day.
MR. : (Inaudible).

Oh, man, that hurt me to my heart. That hurt me worse, and I haven't lied since. I'm not a good, convincing liar today. From that same thing, but I appreciate it. I appreciate it very much. I can't lie anybody. I've got to tell you the truth if it hurts, because I always remember my mother said, if you'll lie, you'll steal.

And I've never stolen anything from anybody, and I don't lie to anybody. (Inaudible) I have to. This is the facts. But this is part of my training in coming up. She was a very firm woman. It hurt her. She was firm with me.
